claim: Chronic restraint stress (RS) application for 2 hours daily for 2 weeks increases immobility in the tail suspension test (TST) in wild-type mice.
source: The behavioral analyses demonstrated that the RS group had increased immobility in both the TST (Figure 1B, Videos 1 and 2; p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests (TST) comparing control and RS groups, with statistical significance (p < 0.001), and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Chronic restraint stress (RS) application for 2 hours daily for 2 weeks increases immobility in the forced swimming test (FST) in wild-type mice.
source: The behavioral analyses demonstrated that the RS group had increased immobility in both the TST (Figure 1B, Videos 1 and 2; p < 0.001) and FST (Figure 1C, Videos 3 and 4; p < 0.001) compared with the CTR group.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests (FST) comparing control and RS groups, with statistical significance (p < 0.001), and is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The increase in immobility due to chronic restraint stress is not due to reduction of general locomotor activity.
source: The increase in immobility is unlikely to be due to the reduction of general locomotor activity, because there was no significant difference in travel distance measured by the OFT between the CTR and the RS groups (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; p = 0.52).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the open-field test (OFT) showing no significant difference in travel distance between control and RS groups (p = 0.52), as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Chronic mild stress by 2 hours of daily restraint stress for 2 weeks triggers behavioral changes assessed by the TST and FST in mice.
source: Through these behavioral tests, we confirmed that chronic mild stress by the application of 2 hr of daily RS for 2 weeks triggers behavioral changes assessed by the TST and FST in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from TST and FST behavioral tests showing increased immobility in stressed mice.

claim: The increase in immobility in the TST and FST has been considered as despair-like behaviors similar to phenotypes observed in patients with depression.
source: The increase in immobility in the TST and FST has been considered as a despair-like behaviors (Wang et al., 2017; Planchez et al., 2019), which is similar to one of phenotypes observed in patients with depression.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Wang et al., 2017; Planchez et al., 2019) that have characterized increased immobility in TST and FST as despair-like behaviors.

claim: Stress-mediated behavioral changes observed in this study are referred to as depression-like behaviors.
source: We refer to the stress-mediated behavioral changes observed in this study as depression-like behaviors that have been used to express behavioral changes triggered by chronic stress in rodent models of depression (Wang et al., 2017; Gururajan et al., 2019; Planchez et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Wang et al., 2017; Gururajan et al., 2019; Planchez et al., 2019) that use the term 'depression-like behaviors' for stress-induced behavioral changes in rodent models.

claim: The expression of c-Fos in the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN) is significantly enhanced after 2 weeks of restraint stress application.
source: The expression of c-Fos in the percentage of all DAPI positive cells for the RS group was significantly enhanced (Figure 1F; p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing increased c-Fos expression in the DCN after RS, with statistical significance (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The expression of c-Fos in the dentate nucleus (DN) is significantly enhanced after 2 weeks of restraint stress application.
source: The expression of c-Fos in the percentage of all DAPI positive cells for the RS group was significantly enhanced (Figure 1F; p < 0.001), particularly in the DN and in the IPN (Figure 1G; DN: p < 0.001; IPN: p = 0.036)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing increased c-Fos expression in the DN after RS, with statistical significance (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The expression of c-Fos in the interposed nucleus (IPN) is significantly enhanced after 2 weeks of restraint stress application.
source: The expression of c-Fos in the percentage of all DAPI positive cells for the RS group was significantly enhanced (Figure 1F; p < 0.001), particularly in the DN and in the IPN (Figure 1G; DN: p < 0.001; IPN: p = 0.036)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing increased c-Fos expression in the IPN after RS, with statistical significance (p = 0.036), as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There is no substantial change in c-Fos level in the fastigial nucleus (FN) after 2 weeks of restraint stress application.
source: In contrast, there was no substantial change in c-Fos level in the FN (Figure 1G; p = 0.74).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing no significant change in c-Fos expression in the FN after RS (p = 0.74), as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The changes in c-Fos expression indicate the activation of DCN neurons in the IPN and the DN by chronic mild stress.
source: This data of the changes in c-Fos expression indicates the activation of DCN neurons in the IPN and the DN by chronic mild stress.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased c-Fos expression (a marker of neuronal activity) in the IPN and DN after chronic stress.

claim: Most c-Fos-positive cells in the DCN are NeuN-positive neurons.
source: Most of the c-Fos-positive cells had an overlap with NeuN (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-staining analysis showing overlap between c-Fos and NeuN (a neuronal marker), as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: c-Fos-positive cells in the DCN are not GAD67-positive.
source: Most of the c-Fos-positive cells had an overlap with NeuN (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), but not with GAD67 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-staining analysis showing no overlap between c-Fos and GAD67 (a marker of inhibitory neurons), as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: c-Fos-positive cells in the DCN are GFAP-negative.
source: As previously reported (Groteklaes et al., 2020), clear signals of GFAP, a marker of glial cells, were not detected in the DCN, and consequently, cFos-positive cells in the DCN were GFAP negative (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-staining analysis showing no GFAP signals in the DCN and no overlap with c-Fos, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, and is consistent with a previous report (Groteklaes et al., 2020).

claim: Cells in the DCN activated by restraint stress are glutamatergic neurons.
source: These results indicate that cells in the DCN activated by RS are glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental data showing that c-Fos-positive cells in the DCN are NeuN-positive (neurons) but not GAD67-positive (inhibitory neurons) or GFAP-positive (glial cells), implying they are excitatory (glutamatergic) neurons.

claim: The c-Fos expression in the DN is significantly enhanced after 3 days of restraint stress application.
source: The c-Fos expression in the RS group was significantly enhanced compared with the CTR group even by 3 days of RS application, and was maintained at elevated level after 7- or 10-day RS application (Figure 1H; 3, 7, or 10 days: p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing increased c-Fos expression in the DN after 3 days of RS, with statistical significance (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The c-Fos expression in the DN is maintained at elevated level after 7 days of restraint stress application.
source: The c-Fos expression in the RS group was significantly enhanced compared with the CTR group even by 3 days of RS application, and was maintained at elevated level after 7- or 10-day RS application (Figure 1H; 3, 7, or 10 days: p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing maintained elevated c-Fos expression in the DN after 7 days of RS, with statistical significance (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The c-Fos expression in the DN is maintained at elevated level after 10 days of restraint stress application.
source: The c-Fos expression in the RS group was significantly enhanced compared with the CTR group even by 3 days of RS application, and was maintained at elevated level after 7- or 10-day RS application (Figure 1H; 3, 7, or 10 days: p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing maintained elevated c-Fos expression in the DN after 10 days of RS, with statistical significance (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Longer restraint stress induces c-Fos expression in more DCN neurons.
source: although the calculation of percentage increase in c-Fos-positive cells over CTR group suggests that longer RS induced c-Fos expression in more DCN neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; p = 0.003).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing a significant increase in the percentage of c-Fos-positive cells with longer RS duration (p = 0.003), as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: DCN neurons in the DN are already activated at the early stage of chronic stress.
source: Thus, the DCN neurons in the DN were already activated at the early stage of chronic stress, suggesting that the DCN neuron activity is involved in stressful situations.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental data showing increased c-Fos expression in the DN after 3 days of RS, indicating early activation of DCN neurons during chronic stress.

claim: DCN neuron activity is involved in stressful situations.
source: Thus, the DCN neurons in the DN were already activated at the early stage of chronic stress, suggesting that the DCN neuron activity is involved in stressful situations.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental data showing increased c-Fos expression (indicating neuronal activity) in the DN during chronic stress.

claim: An increase in activity of DCN neurons in the DN may be relevant to the development of depression-like behaviors.
source: The above-mentioned results raised the possibility that an increase in activity of DCN neurons in the DN may be relevant to the development of depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed correlation between increased DCN neuron activity (c-Fos expression) and depression-like behaviors after chronic stress.

claim: Axons projecting from crus I, crus II, and the simplex lobe are rich in the DN.
source: Previous studies reported that axons projecting from crus I, crus II, and the simplex lobe are rich in the DN (Edge et al., 2003; Tolbert and Bantli, 1978; Voogd et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Edge et al., 2003; Tolbert and Bantli, 1978; Voogd et al., 2012) that reported the anatomical projections from cerebellar cortical regions to the DN.

claim: Crus I is involved in higher brain functions, such as emotion and sociability.
source: Among these cortical regions, crus I is well recognized for its involvement in higher brain functions, such as emotion and sociability (Ferrari et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2020; Tsai et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ferrari et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2020; Tsai et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2007) that have demonstrated the role of crus I in higher brain functions.

claim: Changes in functional connectivity were observed in crus I of patients with depression.
source: Even though the topographic organization of stress-associated responses in the cerebellum is complex, changes in functional connectivity were observed in crus I of patients with depression (Alalade et al., 2011; Depping et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Alalade et al., 2011; Depping et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012) that reported changes in functional connectivity in crus I in patients with depression.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of crus I Purkinje cells using hM3Dq and CNO increases spontaneous firing of Purkinje cells in vitro.
source: Cell-attached recordings from Gq-expressing PCs in cerebellar slices showed increased spontaneous firing after CNO application (10 μM) compared with the baseline, whereas the PCs in the uninfected cerebellum demonstrated no effects of CNO application (Figure 2B; Gq-PCs: t(8) = 3.7, p = 0.003; uninfected PCs: t(14) = 0.19, p = 0.85).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell-attached recordings showing increased firing rate in Gq-expressing PCs after CNO application (p = 0.003), as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Intraperitoneal administration of CNO into mice expressing Gq in Purkinje cells results in increased c-Fos level in Gq-expressing Purkinje cells in crus I in vivo.
source: The increase in activity was also confirmed in vivo by immunohistochemical analysis of c-Fos, which showed that intraperitoneal administration of CNO into mice expressing Gq in PCs resulted in an increased c-Fos level in Gq-expressing PCs in crus I (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing increased c-Fos expression in Gq-expressing PCs after CNO administration, as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Chronic chemogenetic activation of crus I Purkinje cells during restraint stress reduces c-Fos expression in the DN.
source: when we used this chemogenetic tool for enhancing crus I PC activity by the daily injection of CNO for the 2 weeks prior to RS application (Figure 2D), c-Fos expression in the DN was reduced compared with when only RS was applied (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing reduced c-Fos expression in the DN after chronic activation of crus I PCs during RS, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: c-Fos-positive cells in the DN after chronically enhancing the activity of crus I Purkinje cells during restraint stress are significantly decreased to a level equivalent to the control.
source: Quantified data showed that c-Fos-positive cells in the DN after chronically enhancing the activity of crus I PCs during RS were significantly decreased and the level was equivalent to the control (Figure 2F; RS – Gq-CNO: t(11) = –4.25, p < 0.001; CTR – Gq-CNO: t(11) = –0.43, p = 0.67).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification of c-Fos-positive cells showing a significant decrease after chronic activation of crus I PCs during RS (p < 0.001) and no significant difference from control (p = 0.67), as shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CNO administration itself has no effects on restraint stress-dependent depression-like behaviors in mice without expression of chemogenetic molecules.
source: The RS-dependent behavioral changes were not affected by either administration of saline or CNO, as seen by the significantly longer immobile times than the CTR group, but the similar immobile times to the RS group, in both the TST and FST (Figure 2G and H; CTR – RS-Sal, TST: t(41) = 3.91, p < 0.001, FST: t(41) = 3.88, p < 0.001; CTR – RS-CNO, TST: t(42) = 4.01, p < 0.001, FST: t(42) = 3.52, p < 0.001; RS – RS-Sal, TST: t(41) = –0.29, p = 0.77, FST: t(41) = 0.12, p = 0.9; RS – RS-CNO, TST: t(42) = –0.24, p = 0.81, FST: t(42) = –0.29, p = 0.78).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing no significant difference in immobility time between RS-Sal or RS-CNO groups and the RS group (p > 0.05), as shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Saline administration itself has no effects on restraint stress-dependent depression-like behaviors in mice without expression of chemogenetic molecules.
source: The RS-dependent behavioral changes were not affected by either administration of saline or CNO, as seen by the significantly longer immobile times than the CTR group, but the similar immobile times to the RS group, in both the TST and FST (Figure 2G and H; CTR – RS-Sal, TST: t(41) = 3.91, p < 0.001, FST: t(41) = 3.88, p < 0.001; CTR – RS-CNO, TST: t(42) = 4.01, p < 0.001, FST: t(42) = 3.52, p < 0.001; RS – RS-Sal, TST: t(41) = –0.29, p = 0.77, FST: t(41) = 0.12, p = 0.9; RS – RS-CNO, TST: t(42) = –0.24, p = 0.81, FST: t(42) = –0.29, p = 0.78).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing no significant difference in immobility time between RS-Sal group and the RS group (p > 0.05), as shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Intraperitoneal administration of saline or CNO itself has no effects on restraint stress-dependent depression-like behaviors.
source: These results confirm that the intraperitoneal administration of saline or CNO itself has no effects on the RS-dependent depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on experimental data showing no significant effects of saline or CNO administration alone on RS-dependent behavioral changes.

claim: CNO administration to PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the Purkinje cells of crus I shortens the immobile time in the tail suspension test.
source: In contrast, CNO administration to the PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the PCs of crus I, referred to as the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group, but not saline administration (RS-Gq-PC-Sal group), shortened the immobile time in both the TST and FST (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing shortened immobility time in the TST in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group, as shown in Figure 2J.

claim: CNO administration to PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the Purkinje cells of crus I shortens the immobile time in the forced swimming test.
source: In contrast, CNO administration to the PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the PCs of crus I, referred to as the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group, but not saline administration (RS-Gq-PC-Sal group), shortened the immobile time in both the TST and FST (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing shortened immobility time in the FST in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group, as shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group is significantly shorter than that of the RS group in the tail suspension test.
source: Even though there was considerable individual variability in all groups, the average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group was significantly shorter than that of the RS group, but was indistinguishable to the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(51) = –2.18, p = 0.03, FST: t(51) = –2.75, p = 0.007; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(64) = 1.66, p = 0.1, FST: t(64) = –0.12, p = 0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing a significant difference in immobility time between RS-Gq-PC-CNO and RS groups in the TST (p = 0.03), as shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group is significantly shorter than that of the RS group in the forced swimming test.
source: Even though there was considerable individual variability in all groups, the average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group was significantly shorter than that of the RS group, but was indistinguishable to the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(51) = –2.18, p = 0.03, FST: t(51) = –2.75, p = 0.007; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(64) = 1.66, p = 0.1, FST: t(64) = –0.12, p = 0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing a significant difference in immobility time between RS-Gq-PC-CNO and RS groups in the FST (p = 0.007), as shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group is indistinguishable from the CTR group in the tail suspension test.
source: Even though there was considerable individual variability in all groups, the average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group was significantly shorter than that of the RS group, but was indistinguishable to the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(51) = –2.18, p = 0.03, FST: t(51) = –2.75, p = 0.007; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(64) = 1.66, p = 0.1, FST: t(64) = –0.12, p = 0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing no significant difference in immobility time between RS-Gq-PC-CNO and CTR groups in the TST (p = 0.1), as shown in Figure 2J.

source: Even though there was considerable individual variability in all groups, the average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group was significantly shorter than that of the RS group, but was indistinguishable to the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(51) = –2.18, p = 0.03, FST: t(51) = –2.75, p = 0.007; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(64) = 1.66, p = 0.1, FST: t(64) = –0.12, p = 0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing no significant difference in immobility time between RS-Gq-PC-CNO and CTR groups in the FST (p = 0.91), as shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The immobile time in RS-Gq-PC-Sal group is indistinguishable from that of the RS group in the tail suspension test.
source: The immobile time in RS-Gq-PC-Sal group was conversely indistinguishable to that of the RS group, but was significantly longer than the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(51) = –0.57, p = 0.57, FST: t(51) = –0.33, p = 0.74; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(64) = 3.45, p < 0.001, FST: t(64) = 2.55, p = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing no significant difference in immobility time between RS-Gq-PC-Sal and RS groups in the TST (p = 0.57), as shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The immobile time in RS-Gq-PC-Sal group is indistinguishable from that of the RS group in the forced swimming test.
source: The immobile time in RS-Gq-PC-Sal group was conversely indistinguishable to that of the RS group, but was significantly longer than the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(51) = –0.57, p = 0.57, FST: t(51) = –0.33, p = 0.74; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(64) = 3.45, p < 0.001, FST: t(64) = 2.55, p = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing no significant difference in immobility time between RS-Gq-PC-Sal and RS groups in the FST (p = 0.74), as shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The immobile time in RS-Gq-PC-Sal group is significantly longer than the CTR group in the tail suspension test.
source: The immobile time in RS-Gq-PC-Sal group was conversely indistinguishable to that of the RS group, but was significantly longer than the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(51) = –0.57, p = 0.57, FST: t(51) = –0.33, p = 0.74; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(64) = 3.45, p < 0.001, FST: t(64) = 2.55, p = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing a significant difference in immobility time between RS-Gq-PC-Sal and CTR groups in the TST (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 2J.

source: The immobile time in RS-Gq-PC-Sal group was conversely indistinguishable to that of the RS group, but was significantly longer than the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(51) = –0.57, p = 0.57, FST: t(51) = –0.33, p = 0.74; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(64) = 3.45, p < 0.001, FST: t(64) = 2.55, p = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing a significant difference in immobility time between RS-Gq-PC-Sal and CTR groups in the FST (p = 0.01), as shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The open-field test showed unchanged distance movement in all four groups (CTR, RS, RS-Gq-PC-Sal, RS-Gq-PC-CNO).
source: The OFT showed unchanged distance movement in all four groups (Figure 2L; F(3,115) = 0.33, p = 0.33)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the open-field test showing no significant difference in distance traveled among the four groups (p = 0.33), as shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The increase in activity of DCN neurons driven by chronic mild stress promotes the generation of depression-like behaviors.
source: These results in behavior, together with the c-Fos data, suggest that the increase in activity of DCN neurons driven by the chronic mild stress promotes the generation of depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental data showing increased c-Fos expression in DCN neurons after chronic stress and the reduction of depression-like behaviors when DCN neuron activity is suppressed by activating inhibitory PCs.

claim: Excitatory manipulation of crus I Purkinje cell activity during restraint stress application suppresses the generation of depression-like behaviors by inhibiting the activity of DCN neurons in the DN.
source: Consequently, the excitatory manipulation of crus I PC activity during RS application suppressed the generation of depression-like behaviors by inhibiting the activity of DCN neurons in the DN.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental data showing that chemogenetic activation of crus I PCs reduces c-Fos expression in the DN and suppresses depression-like behaviors.

claim: Cerebellar neuronal activity contributes to the stress-dependent development of depression-like behaviors.
source: We hence conclude that cerebellar neuronal activity indeed contributes to the stress-dependent development of depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on experimental data showing that manipulation of cerebellar neuronal activity (crus I PCs) affects the development of depression-like behaviors.

claim: Reciprocal anatomical connections between the cerebellum and VTA have long been known.
source: Reciprocal anatomical connections between these two brain regions have long been known (Snider et al., 1976; Oades and Halliday, 1987; Ikai et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Snider et al., 1976; Oades and Halliday, 1987; Ikai et al., 1992) that reported anatomical connections between the cerebellum and VTA.

claim: GFP-positive axonal projections from the fastigial nucleus (FN) were not observed in the VTA.
source: Upon injection into the FN, GFP-positive axonal projections were not observed in the VTA (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AAV-based tracing showing no GFP-positive axons in the VTA after injection into the FN, as shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Injection of AAV into the interposed nucleus (IPN) displays GFP-positive axons in the red nucleus (RN).
source: Injection to the IPN clearly displayed GFP-positive axons in the red nucleus (RN), which is a well-known projection area from the cerebellum (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AAV-based tracing showing GFP-positive axons in the RN after injection into the IPN, as shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There are weak GFP-positive axonal projections from the IPN in the contralateral side of the dorsolateral anterior VTA.
source: However, there were only weak GFP-positive axonal projections from the IPN in the contralateral side of the dorsolateral anterior VTA and slightly stronger GFP signals in the dorsolateral posterior VTA (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AAV-based tracing showing weak GFP-positive axons in the dorsolateral anterior VTA after injection into the IPN, as shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There are slightly stronger GFP signals from the IPN in the dorsolateral posterior VTA.
source: However, there were only weak GFP-positive axonal projections from the IPN in the contralateral side of the dorsolateral anterior VTA and slightly stronger GFP signals in the dorsolateral posterior VTA (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AAV-based tracing showing slightly stronger GFP signals in the dorsolateral posterior VTA after injection into the IPN, as shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Injection of AAV into the dentate nucleus (DN) displays strong GFP-positive axons in the red nucleus (RN).
source: While the injection into the DN displayed strong GFP-positive axons in the RN, it also resulted in GFP signals mainly in the contralateral side of both the anterior and posterior VTA, and the signals were most abundant compared with the injection into the other two nuclei (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AAV-based tracing showing strong GFP-positive axons in the RN after injection into the DN, as shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Injection of AAV into the dentate nucleus (DN) results in GFP signals mainly in the contralateral side of both the anterior and posterior VTA.
source: While the injection into the DN displayed strong GFP-positive axons in the RN, it also resulted in GFP signals mainly in the contralateral side of both the anterior and posterior VTA, and the signals were most abundant compared with the injection into the other two nuclei (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AAV-based tracing showing GFP signals in the contralateral VTA after injection into the DN, as shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GFP signals from the DN in the VTA are most abundant compared with the injection into the other two nuclei (FN and IPN).
source: While the injection into the DN displayed strong GFP-positive axons in the RN, it also resulted in GFP signals mainly in the contralateral side of both the anterior and posterior VTA, and the signals were most abundant compared with the injection into the other two nuclei (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AAV-based tracing showing the most abundant GFP signals in the VTA after injection into the DN compared to FN and IPN, as shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DCN neurons in the DN project mainly to the dorsolateral posterior VTA among all VTA regions.
source: Particularly, DCN neurons in the DN projected mainly to the dorsolateral posterior VTA among all VTA regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AAV-based tracing showing the most abundant GFP signals in the dorsolateral posterior VTA after injection into the DN.

claim: The projection from the DN and the IPN, but not the FN, to the VTA is consistent with previous studies.
